To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) serum PRL levels increased after 2 or more epileptic seizures in epileptic patient, 2) this increase is more prolonged in patient with temporal ischemia, 3) the increase of serum Prolactin is related with a longer synaptic transmission involved in limbic areas.
the increase of serum Prolactin following repetitive seizures is more prolonged in epileptic patients without than with damage of temporal structures.
the increase of serum Prolactin levels following repetitive temporal epileptic seizure is longer in epileptic patients without temporal damage respect to those with damage of temporal structure.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the analysis of the time course of prolactin increase after repetitive seizures in epileptics with (Group II, n = 10) and without (group I, n = 12) temporal ischemia, in order to investigate the synaptic transmission in the limbic system.
the study of prolactin levels after repetitive epileptic seizures in patients with and without temporal lobe damage.
the analysis of the synaptic transmission involved by the pathways connecting the limbic areas, with the aim to better understand their role in the epileptic process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
prolactin levels are not useful in the diagnosis of seizures in the emergency department.
prolactin levels are elevated following seizures, and that prolactin is a reliable marker for seizure activity in epileptic patients.
the increase in serum prolactin levels is a useful marker in the evaluation of patients with epileptic seizures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

1. the increase in PRL after epileptic seizures is not a consequence of the stress of an epileptic event; 2. the increase in the PRL level after epileptic seizures may reflect a specific activation of the dopaminergic pathways, and; 3. the increase in serum PRL levels may reflect the involvement of different limbic areas in the epileptic seizure.
the PRL response to repetitive seizures is a useful tool to evaluate the synaptic activity in limbic structures.
the long time attenuation of PRL increase after repetitive seizures may be a marker of temporal damage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prolactin is a useful marker in diagnosing epileptic seizures, but it is important to remember that it is not specific to epilepsy.
the increase in PRL following a single seizure is not a useful marker to differentiate between epileptic and non-epileptic events.
prolactin is an important tool in the diagnosis of epileptic seizures.
